chapters.1: Micah announces that God is coming to judge Samaria and Jerusalem for their idolatry, and mourns the coming devastation by naming a string of towns in Judah that will suffer as the disaster spreads toward Jerusalem.
chapters.2: Micah condemns wealthy landowners who scheme at night to seize other people's fields and houses by force, and warns that God will likewise bring disaster on them. He also calls out false prophets who tell people only what they want to hear, while promising a future regathering of a remnant of Israel.
chapters.3: Micah rebukes Israel's corrupt leaders, judges, and false prophets, who exploit the people yet claim nothing bad can happen because God is with them. He contrasts them with his own true calling, filled with the Spirit to confront sin, and warns that Jerusalem's temple mount will become desolate because of their corruption.
chapters.4: Micah envisions a future day when the temple mount will be exalted above all others and nations will stream to it to learn God's ways, with weapons turned into farm tools and lasting peace. He also predicts a coming exile to Babylon from which God will redeem and regather his people.
chapters.5: This chapter contains the famous prophecy that a ruler will come from the small town of Bethlehem, one whose origins are from ancient times, who will shepherd and bring security to God's people. It also promises that the remnant of Israel will eventually prevail over its enemies after God removes the nation's idols and false sources of security.
chapters.6: God brings a legal case against his people, reminding them of all he has done for them since the Exodus and asking what more he could have done. Micah answers that God is not looking for empty ritual sacrifices but for people to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with him, then condemns the dishonest business practices and violence still found in the city.
chapters.7: Micah laments the thorough corruption and betrayal he sees all around him, even within families, but declares he will wait hopefully for God to act on his behalf. The book closes with praise for God's unique willingness to forgive and show mercy, trusting him to fulfill his ancient promises to Israel's ancestors.
